You are a scientific evidence extractor. Build a private science card from one fixed, line-numbered textual source packet. You are not authoring a benchmark case.
Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, without Markdown or extra text.
Use only the supplied source. Do not use outside knowledge or infer missing facts from citations.
Copy the supplied citation, canonical journal DOI, and versioned arXiv ID exactly.
Except for mechanism.variable_names, names and IDs must be ASCII snake-style identifiers. Source-significant uppercase segments such as E_i or T_low may be retained; the next deterministic stage lowercases them for runtime use. mechanism.variable_names may preserve arbitrary raw paper notation.
Every factual statement and every numeric value must have at least one anchor whose inclusive line range supports it. Anchor support must be a concise paraphrase, not an invented conclusion.
Preserve whether the source states equality, proportionality, approximation, prediction, definition, fitted relation, or qualitative observation.
Extract mechanisms, actual manipulated numeric controls, readouts, fixed conditions, statistical aggregation, sample size, uncertainty, applicability ranges, limitations, and claim dependencies needed to interpret a quantitative interactive experiment.
A control is a numeric quantity the study actually manipulates. A readout is a measured or computed observable. Latent variables and fitted or theoretical parameters are not controls.
Sample size, ensemble count, averaging rule, fit method, and uncertainty convention are statistical provenance, not physical fixed conditions and never a hidden-world discriminator. Record them in ScienceReadout.statistic/uncertainty and claim.statistical_basis/uncertainty instead of fixed_conditions. These fields describe the source data; they will not be copied onto a deterministic Oracle query.
Represent source support without inventing continuity: use domain_kind continuous_interval only for a source-supported nonzero interval, numeric_values for explicitly reported discrete manipulated settings, fixed_value for one setting, symbolic for a stated nonnumeric domain, and unreported when the source does not provide one. Only continuous_interval and numeric_values can later compile to Player controls. A fixed value belongs to the experimental context, not a range with equal endpoints. The quantity that distinguishes the two selected source-reported branches is private regime context, not a Player control: represent each branch value or limit as its own branch-specific fixed condition, and make the corresponding claim cite only its branch condition. Two isolated reported condition values do not license interpolation. Never borrow a numeric domain from one claim for another claim merely because they use the same symbol.
Use this exact domain-field table for every control and claim domain: continuous_interval => numeric minimum, numeric maximum with minimum < maximum, allowed_values=[]; numeric_values => minimum=null, maximum=null, at least two unique allowed_values; fixed_value => minimum=null, maximum=null, exactly one allowed_value; symbolic or unreported => minimum=null, maximum=null, allowed_values=[], and a non-empty domain_statement. A one-sided or otherwise non-numeric source condition is not a continuous_interval with a null endpoint. When a reviewer figure-evidence addendum conservatively identifies a finite query set but not a continuous source interval, encode those supported values as numeric_values.
For every quantitative response that could become an Oracle equation, record each fitted coefficient and exponent as a named ScienceParameter under its linked mechanism. The parameter value is the central value; put the paper's uncertainty text in uncertainty. Never leave a numeric coefficient or exponent only inside claim.quantitative_form. If the meaning of a reported plus/minus value is not specified, write source_unspecified; do not guess standard error or confidence interval.
For every retained claim, encode the central-value control-to-readout relation in claim.oracle_outputs using the supplied expression AST. Output keys must exactly equal that claim's readout_names. A {"var": ...} leaf must name one of that claim's control_names. A {"param": ...} leaf must name a ScienceParameter belonging to one of that claim's mechanism_ids. Every scientific constant, including zero or one when it occurs in the source equation, must be a named, anchored ScienceParameter referenced by a param leaf. Numeric literals are forbidden in ScienceClaim oracle_outputs; structural selector literals are added only by the deterministic case binder. Keep quantitative_form as a human-readable rendering of the same relation. Do not put uncertainty ranges into oracle_outputs: the executable Oracle evaluates only source-reported central parameter values. Keep source aggregation, data-point error bars, fit-parameter uncertainty, and their conventions in the provenance fields; they are not uncertainty on each deterministic query result.
An unspecified plus/minus convention is missing metadata, not a contradiction: do not create a source_ambiguity solely because the paper omits whether a quoted fit uncertainty is a standard error, confidence interval, or another convention. Preserve the numeric plus/minus values in the quantitative form and parameter records, mark their meaning source_unspecified, and keep point error bars such as one standard deviation separate when the source defines them.
Parameter names must be globally unique, including after lowercasing. Qualify names by readout and regime when the paper reports several amplitudes, exponents, or other quantities of the same kind.
Keep variable_names in the paper's recognizable notation when useful (for example tau_Q); unlike executable parameter names, they need not be lower_snake_case.
Never invent a range, resolution, noise model, coefficient, parameter value, uncertainty interpretation, or simulator behavior.
Keep general mechanisms and linked empirical claims together rather than atomizing every equation into an unrelated mini-case. claim.mechanism_ids cites mechanisms. claim.depends_on may cite only other claim_ids, never mechanism_ids; use an empty array when a claim has no claim-level prerequisite.
Extract only the single best complete quantitative cluster for this authoring run; do not catalogue a second, unrelated experiment. Prefer two source-reported regimes that can use the same one-to-five controls and one-or-two readouts. If no such pair exists, extract the best single response faithfully and set case_authoring_ready false. Include every fixed condition, statistic, uncertainty, applicability limit, and branch parameter needed to reproduce the selected responses. Every quantitative claim must cite every selected mechanism that supplies a coefficient, exponent, or equation used by that claim. If the same paper symbol has a different meaning or source-supported domain in another experiment, omit that other experiment rather than merging or widening the selected control. Do not exhaust the output budget cataloguing unrelated qualitative results.
Do not bundle a condition that changes between reported regimes into a common fixed condition. Split the common apparatus settings from each regime-specific value, and link each claim only to compatible conditions.
Include only fixed conditions needed to interpret the selected discovery formula. Omit global simulation or acquisition settings that do not enter the selected response, especially when their locator contains a branch-specific value incompatible with the other branch.
Preserve operational definitions separately from captions and fitted relations. A readout anchor must cover how the observable is defined; claim anchors must additionally cover the equation, domain, aggregation, and uncertainty convention they assert. For each claim, control_domains must give one separately anchored source-applicability domain for every cited control, preserving whether it is an interval, discrete values, fixed value, symbolic statement, or unreported; never substitute the broader paper-level control domain. For each readout, resolution is either a separately anchored measurement_resolution/reporting_increment object or null when the source supports neither. Do not infer resolution from uncertainty or silently treat decimal formatting as instrument resolution.
When the paper overloads notation or distinguishes a crossing-relative quantity from an absolute one, create separate readouts or claims and record the ambiguity. Never combine their equations or speculate why one presentation differs.
When main text, caption, appendix, or supplement uses materially different definitions or formulas, record the issue in source_ambiguities and do not silently reconcile it. Link every ambiguity to all affected claims, mechanisms, controls, readouts, and fixed conditions; leave all reference arrays empty only when the ambiguity affects the paper globally.
Set case_authoring_ready true only when the extracted evidence can support at least one numeric control, one numeric readout, one quantitative mechanism, and an objective source-grounded response within an explicit domain.
Do not generate Player background, initial observations, episode budgets, diagnostic or hidden conditions, counterfactuals, or code. The claim.oracle_outputs source relation is the only expression tree requested at this extraction stage.

Delete the .0088-versus-.029 source ambiguity because .0088 is an external experiment. The mu_f=.80 claim must cite both the parameter table and Figure 6 / source lines 340-375 supporting the same fit form and applicability. mu_c plus/minus convention is source_unspecified provenance only and is not propagated to each normalized r value. No extra claims.
This hint only selects a part of the supplied source for inspection. Verify every extracted fact against that source and provide exact locators; the source remains the sole authority. If the hinted cluster is unsupported or incomplete, represent it faithfully and set case_authoring_ready false.

L000094	\begin{abstract}
L000095	We present particle-resolved simulations of dense frictional suspensions undergoing the viscous-inertial transition using pressure-imposed rheology.
L000096	
L000097	By varying the fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular pressure, we find that the transition is independent of the packing fraction and occurs at a Stokes number of 10.
L000098	
L000099	Our results reveal that the shear stress exhibits a slower transition than the particle pressure, attributed to the combined effect of tangential contact and lubrication forces, as the frictional particles concurrently shift from rolling to sliding contacts. This shift is controlled by the Stokes number but also by the distance from jamming.
L000100	
L000101	Additionally, we examine the role of increasing inter-particle friction on the viscous-inertial transition.
L000102	
L000103	\end{abstract}
L000104	
L000105

L000108	\maketitle
L000109	
L000110	
L000111	\textit{Introduction:} Flows of dense suspensions are ubiquitous in nature and industrial applications \cite{vowinckel2021incorporating}. Their behaviors are very complex and far from being fully understood across flow regimes \cite{guazzelli2018rheology}.
L000112	
L000113	In the viscous regime, the rheology is controlled by the dimensionless number $J$, defined as $J=\eta_f \dot \gamma / P$, the ratio of the viscous stress scale to the confining pressure, with $\eta_f$, $\dot \gamma$ and $P$ being fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular (confining) pressure \cite{boyer2011unifying}.
L000114	
L000115	Inertial flows are characterized by an analogous dimensionless quantity $I$, defined as $I^2 = \rho_p d^2 \dot \gamma ^2/ P$, the ratio of the inertial stress scale to the confining pressure, with $\rho_p$ and $d$ being particle density and diameter, respectively \cite{forterre2008flows}.
L000116	
L000117	A few experimental \cite{bagnold1954,fall2010transition, madraki2020shear, tapia2022viscous}, theoretical and numerical \cite{trulsson2012transition, ness2015flow, DeGiuli2015transition, DeGiuli2016phaseDiagram, trulsson2017friction, amarsid2017viscoinertial, vo2020additive} studies have focused on understanding the rheology in the transition between the viscous and inertial regimes.
L000118	
L000119	Although relevant to many environmental and engineering flows \cite{jerolmack2019viewing,ness2022physics}, there remains little consensus on a unified framework for the viscous-inertial transition, posing challenges for conventional two-phase flow modeling approaches \cite{ouriemi2009sediment,chauchat2017sedfoam}.
L000120	
L000121	
L000122	
L000123	\citet{trulsson2012transition} suggested that the packing fraction $\phi$ and macroscopic friction coefficient $\mu$ are governed by a single dimensionless number $K = J + \alpha I^2$  in the viscous-inertial regime, with $\alpha= 1/St_{v \rightarrow i}$ where $St_{v \rightarrow i}$ is the Stokes number at which the viscous to inertial transition occurs.
L000124	
L000125	The Stokes number $St$ is defined as the ratio of inertial to viscous stress scales $I^2/J$.
L000126	
L000127	Other numerical studies \cite{amarsid2017viscoinertial, ness2015flow} with frictional non-colloidal spheres agree well with the findings of \citet{trulsson2012transition} and report that the viscous-inertial transition occurs at $St_{v \rightarrow i} = 1-2 $.
L000128	
L000129	In contrast, experiments with frictionless colloidal spheres reported that $St_{v \rightarrow i} \rightarrow 0$ when approaching the jamming transition \cite{fall2010transition, madraki2020shear}, which is consistent with the theory of \citet{DeGiuli2015transition}.
L000130	
L000131	Conversely, for frictional spheres,  \citet{tapia2022viscous} found that the transition occurs at $St_{v \rightarrow i} = 10 $ independent of $\phi$, consistent with the seminal experiments of \citet{bagnold1954}.
L000132	
L000133	Another significant observation in \cite{tapia2022viscous} is that $\phi$ and $\mu$ are governed by two different values for $\alpha$ ($\alpha_{\phi} = 0.1$ and $\alpha_{\mu}=0.0088$) reflecting the slower transition of the shear stress compared to the granular pressure.
L000134	
L000135	These differing values of $\alpha$ are maintained for a suspension consisting of soft spheres having low interparticle friction \cite{tapia2024soft}.
L000136	
L000137	Numerical studies \cite{trulsson2012transition, ness2015flow, amarsid2017viscoinertial, vo2020additive} have not yet captured this behavior.
L000138	
L000139	
L000140	In this work, we perform particle resolved simulations using pressure-imposed rheology and show that the combined effect of tangential contact and lubrication forces are responsible for the two distinct scalings of $\phi$ and $\mu$ observed by \citet{tapia2022viscous}.
L000141	
L000142	We also demonstrate that the slower transition in $\mu$ is governed by the rolling-to-sliding transition in the contact network, which depends on viscosity and distance from jamming.
L000143	
L000144	Previous numerical works \cite{trulsson2012transition, ness2015flow, amarsid2017viscoinertial} underestimate the magnitude of tangential contact force and lubrication, leading to the absence of two different scalings for $\phi$ and $\mu$.
L000145	
L000146	
L000147	\textit{Numerical Method:} The flow behavior of the suspension is analyzed using particle-resolved computational fluid dynamics simulations.
L000148	
L000149	Our simulations integrate the discrete element method (DEM) to model particle dynamics and the immersed boundary method (IBM) to resolve the fluid flow.
L000150	
L000151	The collision model for particle dynamics is adapted from the work of \citet{biegert2017collision}.
L000152	
L000153	
L000154	
L000155	The model involves lubrication forces $\mbs{F}_{l}$, normal contact forces $\mbs{F}_{n}$ and frictional contact forces $\mbs{F}_{t}$, to provide the total collision force between neighboring particles $p$ and $q$ as $\textbf{F}_{c,p} =\textbf{F}_{l,pq} + \textbf{F}_{n,pq} + \textbf{F}_{t,pq}$. With the lubrication force represented as,
L000156	
L000157	\begin{equation}\label{eq:lubrication}
L000158	
L000159		\textbf{F}_{l} = \frac{6 \pi \eta_f R_{eff}^2}{max(\zeta_n,\zeta_{n,min})} \hspace{0.5cm},
L000160	
L000161	\end{equation}
L000162	
L000163	where, $\zeta_n$ is the gap size of two interacting particles, $\zeta_{n,min}$ is the critical value below which the lubrication forces are kept constant, and $R_{eff}$ is the effective radius accounting for polydispersity.
L000164	
L000165	The repulsive normal component is represented by a nonlinear spring-dashpot model
L000166	
L000167	\begin{equation} \label{eq:acm_force}
L000168	\textbf{F}_{n,pq} = -k_n |\zeta_n|^{3/2} \textbf{n} - d_n \textbf{g}_{n,cp} \qquad ,
L000169	\end{equation}
L000170	
L000171	where, $d_n$ and $k_n$ represent damping and stiffness coefficients respectively, adjusted to obtain a restitution coefficient $e_c$.
L000172	
L000173	The normal vector pointing toward the collision partner is given by \textbf{n}, and \textbf{g}$_{n,cp}$ is the normal component of the relative particle velocity at the contact point.
L000174	
L000175	\begin{figure}[b]
L000176	\includegraphics[width=0.48\textwidth]{Figure_1.pdf}
L000177	\caption{\label{fig:setup_rheology} Rheological data of the pressure-imposed rheometry with the $3$ different fluid viscosities $\eta_f = 10, 100, 1000$. (a) $\phi/\phi_c$ vs $K_{\phi}$ with fits corresponding to $\phi = \phi_c(1 - a_\phi K_\phi ^{1/2})$ with $a_\phi = 0.62$; the inset shows snapshot of the setup used in this work. (b) $\mu/\mu_c$ vs $K_{\phi}$ with fits $\mu = \mu_c(1 + a_\mu K_\phi ^{1/2})$ with distinct $a_\mu$ for each viscosity; the inset provides $\mu/\mu_c$ vs $K_\mu$ with a single fit $\mu = \mu_c (1 + a_\mu K_\mu ^{1/2}) $ with $a_{\mu}=14.3$. }
L000178	\end{figure}
L000179	
L000180	The tangential forces are given by
L000181	
L000182	\begin{equation} \label{eq:lin_tan}
L000183	\textbf{F}_{t,pq} = \min \left(-k_t  \boldsymbol{\zeta}_t - d_t \textbf{g}_{t,cp} , ||\mu_f \textbf{F}_n|| \textbf{t} \right)  \qquad ,
L000184	\end{equation}
L000185	
L000186	which takes the minimum of either the rolling (1st term on the right hand side)  or the sliding (2nd term) components.
L000187	
L000188	In Eq.\,(\ref{eq:lin_tan}), $\mu_f$ represents the friction coefficient between the two surfaces and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}_t$ is the tangential displacement accumulated during the contact time between two particles \citep{thornton2013investigation}.
L000189	
L000190	Further, \textbf{g}$_{t,cp}$ is the tangential component of the relative surface velocities and \textbf{t} points in the direction of the tangential force.
L000191	
L000192	
L000193	The parameters $e_c=0.97$ and $\mu_f=0.15$ (which is our reference $\mu_f$) have been taken from experiments involving glass spheres \cite{gondret2002bouncing,joseph2004oblique}.
L000194	
L000195	The computational domain closely replicates the apparatus of \citet{tapia2022viscous} for pressure-imposed rheology.
L000196	
L000197	The shear cell has dimensions $L_x\times L_y \times L_z=10 d\times 10.6 d \times 10 d$ and a grid resolution of $N_x\times N_y \times N_z= 200\times 212 \times 200$.
L000198	
L000199	It consists of 871 neutrally buoyant monodisperse particles (with a diameter variance of $5\%$ to prevent crystallization) in a viscous fluid.
L000200	
L000201	These particles are sheared by top and bottom plates, i.e., the red particles in the inset of Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}(a), with a shear rate $\dot \gamma$ thereby imposing a linear shear profile.
L000202	
L000203	Each plate comprises 49 particles, for a total of 98 plate particles.
L000204	
L000205	The plate particles are larger than those in the suspension ($1.3 d$) and form porous walls.
L000206	
L000207	Each particle of the top plate is assigned a weight to exert granular pressure $P$ on the suspension.
L000208	
L000209	A no-slip condition is applied on the shearing walls and on the particle surface. Periodic boundary conditions are applied in the flow and vorticity directions.
L000210	
L000211	A reservoir space between the top plate particles and the top wall enables movement in the velocity-gradient direction in response to the suspension dilating or compacting under shear.
L000212	
L000213	The volume fraction $\phi$ is determined by the distance measured between the two horizontal planes cutting the top and bottom plate spheres at their center.
L000214	
L000215	The volume occupied by the plate particles is excluded, ensuring that only the volume available for particle flow is considered.
L000216	
L000217	
L000218	
L000219

(a) $\mu_h/\mu_c$ versus $K_\phi$ with $b=0$ and $n=1.5$, inset shows $\mu_n/\mu_c$ with $b=1$ and $n=0.5$, (b) $\mu_t/\mu_c$ versus $K_\phi$ with $b=0.04$ and $n=0.75$.}

L000232	
L000233	
L000234	\textit{Results:}
L000235	
L000236	We performed simulations with three different viscosities $\eta_f = 10, 100, 1000$ at varying $\dot \gamma$, where $\eta_f$ is normalized by the viscosity of water.
L000237	
L000238	The range of $St$ numbers in this study is $0.01-300$.
L000239	
L000240	We evaluated the shear stress $\tau$ due to contact, lubrication and long-range hydrodynamic forces (volume averaged) on the top and bottom plate particles.
L000241	
L000242	The rheological data and plots are given in the Supplemental Material \footnote{See Supplemental Material at http://.}.
L000243	
L000244	
L000245	
L000246	To investigate the transition, we adopt the definition of \citet{tapia2022viscous} and use $K=K_{\phi}=J+\alpha_{\phi} I^2$, where $\alpha_{\phi}=1/St_{v\rightarrow i}=0.1$.
L000247	
L000248	The rheological data for $\phi$ and $\mu$ in Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology} are normalized by their critical values $\phi_c=0.60 \pm 0.02$ and $\mu_c = 0.30 \pm 0.02$ at jamming, obtained by fitting $1-\phi/\phi_c$ and $\mu/\mu_c -1$ with $K^{1/2}$.
L000249	
L000250	The data for $\phi$ collapse, indicating a uniform transition of $P$ from the viscous to the inertial regime at $St_{v\rightarrow i}=10$, while those for $\mu$ do not.
L000251	
L000252	They collapse when plotted against a different $K$ defined as $K_{\mu}= J + \alpha_{\mu} I^2$ with $\alpha_{\mu} = 0.029$ which yields a different transitional Stokes number of $St_{v\rightarrow i}^{\mu}=35$, as shown in the inset of Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}(b).
L000253	
L000254	These numerical results recover the transition at a Stokes number $St_{v\rightarrow i}=10$ independent of $\phi$ found experimentally by \citet{tapia2022viscous} for spheres suspended in water-UCON oil mixture with an interparticle friction $\mu_f= 0.14$ \cite{Tapia2023erratum} similar to the present reference $\mu_f= 0.15$.
L000255	
L000256	In addition, they show a different scaling for $\mu$ with a larger transitional $St_{v\rightarrow i}^{\mu}$. This qualitatively agrees with the experiments, although the numerical $St_{v\rightarrow i}^{\mu}(=35)$ is smaller than the experimental $St_{v\rightarrow i}^{\mu}(=114)$, which may be attributed to the confinement, lubrication and friction models used in the present simulations.
L000257	
L000258	
L000259	
L000260	We turn to understand the origin of the distinct $St_{v\rightarrow i}$ values for the transition of $\phi$ and $\mu$.
L000261	
L000262	The macroscopic friction coefficient $\mu$, shown in Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}(b), can be decomposed into its three components presented separately in Fig.\,\ref{fig:stress_decomposition}: normal contact $\mu_n$, tangential contact $\mu_t$, and hydrodynamics $\mu_h$ (including both lubrication and long-range hydrodynamic interactions).
L000263	
L000264	Clearly, the normal contribution $\mu_n (K_{\phi})/\mu_c$ (in the inset) is devoid of the diverging behavior, implying that normal contact forces are not responsible for the differing scaling of $\mu$.
L000265	
L000266	Conversely, the hydrodynamic contribution $\mu_h (K_{\phi})/\mu_c$, which is dominated by lubrication, is negligible for low $K_{\phi}$ values, but exhibits a divergent trend at large $K_{\phi}$ values where it becomes comparable to the friction forces.
L000267	
L000268	The tangential component $\mu_t (K_{\phi})/\mu_c$ has its maximum divergence with $K_{\phi}$ compared to $\mu_n (K_{\phi})$ and $\mu_h (K_{\phi})$.
L000269	
L000270	Thus, we argue that $\mu_t$ triggers the influence of lubrication forces and is responsible for the differing scaling of $\mu$.
L000271	
L000272	
L000273	
L000274	To this end, we probe the role of tangential contact forces by analyzing two simulation runs with the same $K$-value ($K=0.065$) which result in different $\mu$ values, as shown in Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}(b).
L000275	
L000276	The Stokes numbers corresponding to the viscosities $\eta_f=1000$ and $10$ are $St =0.65$ and $206.5$, respectively.
L000277	
L000278	The snapshots given in Figs.\,\ref{fig:force_networks}(a) and \ref{fig:force_networks}(d) show the force networks in the suspensions for the tangential components in the steady state of the simulations normalized by the mean total contact force recorded for the respective snapshot.
L000279	
L000280	Figs.\,\ref{fig:force_networks}(a) and \ref{fig:force_networks}(d) illustrate the characteristic network for the viscous and inertial regimes, respectively.
L000281	
L000282	Clearly, the force network of the tangential forces becomes weaker with higher $St$.
L000283	
L000284	Using Eq.\,\eqref{eq:lin_tan}, we further decompose this force network into rolling and sliding components. This is illustrated in Figs.\,\ref{fig:force_networks}(b) and \ref{fig:force_networks}(c) for $\eta_f=1000$.
L000285	
L000286	For this simulation run, most of the network structure is formed by rolling contacts, where the individual forces are strong and well connected throughout the entire suspension.
L000287	
L000288	At the same time, the sliding contact forces are smaller in magnitude and sparse.
L000289	
L000290	The spatial pattern of the network distribution completely changes as the viscosity is decreased by two orders of magnitude, see Figs.\,\ref{fig:force_networks}(e) and \ref{fig:force_networks}(f).
L000291	
L000292	Here, the rolling contacts become less important, because they are sparse, whereas the fabric of the suspension is now supported by the network of sliding contacts.
L000293	
L000294	Nevertheless, the magnitude of rolling contact is higher than that of sliding, even for higher $St$.
L000295	
L000296	In summary, the suspension transits from having rolling contacts in the viscosity dominant regime to sliding contacts in the inertial regime for the same $K$-value.
L000297	
L000298	
L000299	\begin{figure}
L000300	\includegraphics[width=0.465\textwidth]{Figure_4.pdf}
L000301	\caption{\label{fig:rolling_sliding} Variation of the fraction of sliding to rolling contacts $\chi$, (a) with $St$ satisfying the function $\chi(St)= (c\cdot St)/(1+ c\cdot St)$ and (b) as a function of $St$ and $\Delta \phi /\phi_c$, the distance from jamming, $\chi(St, \, \Delta \phi /\phi_c)= (St \, \Delta \phi /\phi_c)^{1/2}/[1+ (St \, \Delta \phi /\phi_c)^{1/2}]$.
L000302	}
L000303	\end{figure}
L000304	
L000305	
L000306	We now evaluate the influence of $St$ on the ratio of the total number of sliding to rolling contacts $\chi$ \cite{trulsson2017friction, DeGiuli2015transition, DeGiuli2016phaseDiagram} in Fig.\,\ref{fig:rolling_sliding}(a).
L000307	
L000308	We obtain different shifted curves with decreasing viscosities corresponding to the diminishing slope with $K_{\phi}^{1/2}$ in Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}(b).
L000309	
L000310	Strikingly, the rolling-to-sliding transition occurs at lower $St$ for higher viscosities. For the largest viscosity, the distance from jamming $\Delta \phi=(\phi_c-\phi)$ is small and the contact network is dominated by rolling contacts. Conversely, for the lowest viscosity, $\Delta \phi$ is larger and sliding contacts prevail.
L000311	
L000312	Based on this observation, the data can be collapsed in Fig.\,\ref{fig:rolling_sliding}(b) into a single curve by rescaling $St$ with $St \, \Delta \phi /\phi_c$ and using a power law of $1/2$, which is also equivalent to using $(St K_{\phi}^{1/2})^{1/2}$.
L000313	
L000314	This illustrates that the transitional $St$ is governed by the rolling-to-sliding transition and the distance from jamming.
L000315	
L000316	
L000317	\begin{figure}
L000318	\includegraphics[width=0.43\textwidth]{Figure_5.pdf}
L000319	\caption{\label{fig:topplate_response} Granular pressure $P$ (a) and the corresponding volume fraction $\phi$ variation (b) of the simulations for several strain units, $\dot{\gamma} \delta t$, in the well-developed state at $St=0.0125$, $20$, and $120$ represented by brown, black and purple lines respectively. $\bar\phi$ and $\bar P$ are the mean values for the respective $St$.}
L000320	\end{figure}
L000321	
L000322	
L000323	The macroscopic response of the pressure-imposed shear cell to changes in the supension microstructure over a few strain units (in the well-developed state) can be seen in Fig.\,\ref{fig:topplate_response}. The analysis is presented for three Stokes numbers ($St=0.0125$, $20$, and $120$), representing one at each extreme of the viscous and inertial regimes and an intermediate value. Fig.\,\ref{fig:topplate_response}(a) shows P acting on the top plate, whereas the response of $\phi$ is shown in Fig.\,\ref{fig:topplate_response}(b).
L000324	
L000325	At $St=0.0125$, strong rolling contacts create a dense network that couples plate motion to pressure fluctuations. At higher $St$, this coupling weakens, and the system becomes more fluidized (at $St = 120$), with sliding contacts leading to less fluctuations of the top plate.
L000326	
L000327	A movie showing the two simulation runs of  $St=0.0125,120$ is given in \footnote{See movie at http://.}.
L000328	
L000329	These results underscore the role of microstructural transitions from rolling-to-sliding in controlling the macroscopic behavior.

L000364	
L000365	Finally, in Fig.\,\ref{fig:changing_fric} we investigate the effect of increasing the interparticle friction coefficient $\mu_f$ above the reference case ($\mu_f=0.15$) on the viscous-inertial transition as described in Fig.\,\ref{fig:setup_rheology}.
L000366	
L000367	A result of interest is that $\mu_c$ is not significantly affected by varying $\mu_f$ while $\phi_c$ slightly decreases
L000368	with increasing $\mu_f$, consistent with experiments \cite{Tapia2019roughness}.
L000369	
L000370	The data for $\phi$ collapse for all studied $\mu_f= 0.15,0.5, 0.8$ using the same $\alpha_{\phi} = 0.1$ in Fig.\,\ref{fig:changing_fric}(a). This implies that the transitional Stokes number remains $St_{v \rightarrow i} = 10$, still in agreement with the experiments of \citet{tapia2022viscous}.
L000371	
L000372	Conversely, $\mu$ shows different curves when plotted against $K_\phi$ in Fig.\,\ref{fig:changing_fric}(b) with a shift of increasing magnitude for the large-viscosity curves with increasing $\mu_f$. The curves for $\mu$ collapse when plotted against $K_{\mu}= J + \alpha_{\mu} I^2$ as seen as an example in the inset for $\mu_f=0.5$ but with values for $\alpha_{\mu}$ which are decreasing with increasing $\mu_f$.
L000373	Thus, $\mu$ which encapsulates the response of the anisotropy of the stresses shows transition that is affected by the interparticle friction as $St^{\mu}_{v \rightarrow i}$ increases with increasing $\mu_f$ ($St^{\mu}_{v \rightarrow i}=35, 64, 114$ for $\mu_f=0.15, 0.5, 0.8$ respectively).
L000374	
L000375	Interestingly, quantitative agreement with the experimental value of $St^{\mu}_{v \rightarrow i}$ \cite{tapia2022viscous} can only be achieved by using a much higher $\mu_f$.
L000376	
L000377	
L000378	\textit{Conclusion:} We have investigated the rheological response of dense suspensions close to jamming at the viscous-inertial transition.
L000379	
L000380	The primary outcome of our particle resolved simulations is that the transition of the granular pressure $P$ which is reflected in $\phi$ does indeed occur at $St_{v \rightarrow i}=10$, in quantitative agreement with the experiments of \citet{tapia2022viscous}.
L000381	The second result is the qualitative agreement with the different transition in $\mu$ which indicates a slower transition of $\tau$ compared to that of $P$.
L000382	Our numerical simulations rationalize the idea presented in \citet{tapia2022viscous} that the change in the nature of the particle interactions is responsible for the transitional behavior of $\mu$ by clearly showing that the viscous-inertial transition is related to the suspension transiting from rolling to sliding.
L000383	
L000384	This slower transition is due to the combined effect of tangential contact and lubrication forces.
L000385	
L000386	We show that the rolling-to-sliding transition is governed not only by the Stokes number, but also by the distance from jamming.
L000387	
L000388	
L000389	Previous numerical studies \cite{amarsid2017viscoinertial, ness2015flow, trulsson2012transition} have not explored the influence of the distance from jamming and underestimated the combined contribution of the tangential and lubrication force components.
L000390	
L000391	Finally, increasing the interparticle friction does not seem to affect the transition in $\phi$ but it impacts the transition in $\mu$.  Further investigation is needed to determine the extent of this effect, as well as to investigate decreasing the friction toward the frictionless limit.
